propositions.text: The appellant, Jennifer Virgo, has appealed a Federal Court order dated December 17, 2018, which upheld a Prothonotary's order.
propositions.quote: The appellant, Jennifer Virgo, has brought an appeal to this Court from an order of the Federal Court dated December 17, 2018, which upheld an earlier order by a Prothonotary.

propositions.text: There is a serious problem with this appeal requiring action due to a flagrant breach of a vexatious litigant order.
propositions.quote: However, there is now a most serious problem with this appeal. Action has to be taken. Vexatious litigant order flagrantly breached

paragraphs.summary: The appellant appealed a Federal Court order, but a serious problem exists due to a flagrant breach of a vexatious litigant order, says the court.

propositions.text: Ade Olumide, spouse of appellant Jennifer Virgo, was declared a vexatious litigant by this Court in 2017.
propositions.quote: Ade Olumide has been declared a vexatious litigant by this Court: Canada v. Olumide, 2017 FCA 42, [2018] 2 F.C.R. 328.

propositions.text: The vexatious litigant order prohibits Ade Olumide from starting new proceedings without leave, acting personally or through others.
propositions.quote: In declaring Ade Olumide a vexatious litigant, this Court prohibited him from starting new proceedings without leave, whether acting for himself or through others.

paragraphs.summary: The court states Ade Olumide was declared a vexatious litigant and prohibited from starting new proceedings without leave.

propositions.text: Ade Olumide is litigating through Jennifer Virgo without seeking leave, breaching the vexatious litigant order flagrantly.
propositions.quote: Ade Olumide is litigating his interests through Jennifer Virgo. He has not sought leave to do so. Therefore, he is breaching the prohibition contained in the vexatious litigant order against him. And the breach is flagrant.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Ade Olumide is flagrantly breaching the vexatious litigant order by litigating through Jennifer Virgo without leave.

propositions.text: The Prothonotary and Federal Court found Jennifer Virgo's name disguises Ade Olumide as the directing mind behind the proceedings.
propositions.quote: both the Prothonotary and the Federal Court found that Jennifer Virgo’s name was “a thin veneer to disguise [Ade] Olumide as the directing mind behind these proceedings.”

propositions.text: These findings are not challenged in this Court.
propositions.quote: These findings are not challenged in this Court.

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision-makers found Virgo's name disguises Olumide as the directing mind; this is unchallenged in this Court.

propositions.text: The Prothonotary and Federal Court findings understate the situation; Ade Olumide is the true appellant, not Jennifer Virgo.
propositions.quote: The findings of the Prothonotary and the Federal Court are understated. The situation is much worse. The material filed shows that the true appellant is Ade Olumide, not Jennifer Virgo.

propositions.text: Jennifer Virgo has no interest in the appeal; documents filed by her are authored by Ade Olumide, as shown by style and explicit acknowledgments.
propositions.quote: Jennifer Virgo has no interest in this appeal. Only Ade Olumide has an interest in it. The documents filed supposedly by Jennifer Virgo are those of Ade Olumide; indeed, on some documents he explicitly acknowledges his authorship. Further evidence of authorship is seen by the style of reasoning and writing in the documents.

propositions.text: Ade Olumide has started a new proceeding without leave, acting through others, breaching the vexatious litigant order.
propositions.quote: Ade Olumide has started a new proceeding without leave, acting through others, and, thus, has breached the vexatious litigant order.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Ade Olumide is the true appellant, authoring documents filed by Virgo, breaching the vexatious litigant order by starting proceedings without leave.

propositions.text: Serious consequences are now live; background shows the Court gave Ade Olumide and Jennifer Virgo full opportunity to explain and address conduct.
propositions.quote: Certain serious consequences are now live. Before discussing them, I wish to describe some of the background leading up to this matter. The background shows that this Court has given Ade Olumide and Jennifer Virgo a full and fair opportunity to offer explanations for their conduct and to address the consequences of their conduct.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes serious consequences are live and that it gave Ade Olumide and Virgo full opportunity to explain their conduct.

propositions.text: Four weeks ago, a motion by Jennifer Virgo was before the Court; the Court suspected Ade Olumide was litigating through her, as respondent also indicated.
propositions.quote: Roughly four weeks ago, a motion said to be brought by Jennifer Virgo was placed before the Court for decision. Within seconds of reviewing the motion materials, the Court apprehended that Ade Olumide may be litigating his interests through Jennifer Virgo contrary to the vexatious litigant order. The respondent certainly made this clear, as he has in previous motions brought in this appeal.

paragraphs.summary: The court recalls a motion by Virgo raised suspicion that Olumide was litigating through her, as respondent also indicated.

propositions.text: Rule 74 requires removal of documents filed contrary to Court orders, but only after submissions and if warranted.
propositions.quote: Rule 74 provides that a document that is filed contrary to an order of the Court “must be removed from the Court file.” But Rule 74 also provides that this can happen only after the parties have been given an opportunity to make submissions and only where it is warranted.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains Rule 74 requires removal of documents filed contrary to Court orders, but only after submissions and if warranted.

propositions.text: The Court has plenary powers to restrain abuses of process and stop meritless proceedings, as superior courts of record.
propositions.quote: this Court’s plenary powers—the powers all courts have by virtue of their status and function as courts... allow the Court to restrain abuses of its process and to stop meritless proceedings in their tracks.

paragraphs.summary: The court states it has plenary powers to restrain abuses of process and stop meritless proceedings as a superior court of record.

propositions.text: The Court issued a direction under Rule 74, stating preliminary view that appeal is contrary to vexatious litigant order and invited evidence and representations.
propositions.quote: Acting under Rule 74, the Court issued a direction. In it, the Court stated its preliminary view that the appeal was contrary to the vexatious litigant order against Ade Olumide. The Court gave the parties named in this appeal and Ade Olumide an opportunity to file evidence and written representations on the matter.

propositions.text: The Court asked five specific questions about the appeal's factual basis, Virgo's interest, breach of order, removal of appeal, and further directions.
propositions.quote: In particular, the Court asked the parties to address five questions: 1. Does the notice of appeal put in issue the factual statements made by the Federal Court judge and the Prothonotary relating to Mr. Olumide’s involvement in this appeal? ... 5. If so, should any other directions and orders be made to prevent a recurrence of this conduct?

paragraphs.summary: The court issued a direction under Rule 74, stating its preliminary view and asking five questions for evidence and representations.

propositions.text: Jennifer Virgo and Ade Olumide did not file evidence or representations to rebut the Court's preliminary view; only the Attorney General filed representations.
propositions.quote: Jennifer Virgo and Ade Olumide were invited to file first. They did not file anything. ... The Attorney General then filed representations. Jennifer Virgo and Ade Olumide did not file representations in reply.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes Virgo and Olumide did not file evidence or representations; only the Attorney General filed representations.

propositions.text: The Court is satisfied Virgo and Olumide had full and fair opportunity to address the matter.
propositions.quote: For the foregoing reasons, the Court is satisfied that Jennifer Virgo and Ade Olumide have had a full and fair opportunity to speak to this matter and influence the Court’s decision-making.

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes Virgo and Olumide had full and fair opportunity to address the matter.

propositions.text: A preliminary issue is whether one judge or three judges should decide this matter.
propositions.quote: One other preliminary issue needs to be addressed: the composition of the Court to deal with this matter. Can this matter be determined by one judge or must it be determined by three judges of this Court?

propositions.text: One judge of this Court can deal with this matter.
propositions.quote: For the following reasons, one judge of this Court can deal with this matter.

paragraphs.summary: The court raises and decides that one judge can deal with this matter.

propositions.text: Section 16 of the Federal Courts Act requires three judges for appeals unless otherwise provided; this matter is not an appeal hearing.
propositions.quote: Section 16 of the Federal Courts Act provides that “[e]xcept as otherwise provided in [the] Act…every appeal…shall be heard…before not fewer than three judges sitting together.” Otherwise, a single judge may suffice. Is the matter before the Court a hearing of an appeal? No.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains s.16 FCA requires three judges for appeals unless otherwise provided; this is not an appeal hearing.

propositions.text: A single judge can make or address vexatious litigant orders under s.40 FCA, including non-compliance issues.
propositions.quote: A single judge can make a vexatious litigant order under section 40: see, e.g., Olumide, above. It stands to reason that a single judge can address the issue of how to deal with non-compliance with that order, including whether the order needs to be amended or supplemented.

paragraphs.summary: The court states a single judge can make or address vexatious litigant orders under s.40 FCA, including breaches.

propositions.text: Rule 74 can be used to remove the notice of appeal and close the file to ensure compliance with the vexatious litigant order, not to dispose of the appeal on merits.
propositions.quote: such an order effectively terminates the appeal. But the order is merely a way of ensuring compliance with the vexatious litigant order and in no way disposes of the appeal on its merits.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains Rule 74 removal of appeal is to ensure compliance, not to dispose of the appeal on merits.

propositions.text: Rule 74 can also terminate appeals for lack of jurisdiction, which is different from enforcing vexatious litigant orders.
propositions.quote: This is different from the use of Rule 74 to terminate an appeal because the Court has no jurisdiction to hear it: see, e.g., Rock-St Laurent v. Canada ... Wong v. Canada ... When Rule 74 is used in those circumstances, the Court considers its ability to hear the appeal—a matter going to the appeal’s merits.

paragraphs.summary: The court distinguishes Rule 74 use to terminate appeals for jurisdictional reasons from its use to enforce vexatious litigant orders.

propositions.text: The Court now considers the severe potential consequences of breaching the vexatious litigant order.
propositions.quote: Now to the potential consequences that can follow from the breach of the vexatious litigant order. They are among the most severe possible in a free and democratic society.

paragraphs.summary: The court introduces the severe potential consequences of breaching the vexatious litigant order.

propositions.text: The Court can start contempt proceedings against Ade Olumide for breaching the vexatious litigant order, including imprisonment, fines, orders, seizure, and costs.
propositions.quote: This Court can start contempt proceedings against Ade Olumide for breaching the vexatious litigant order. ... imprisonment for up to five years, a fine of any amount justified by the circumstances, an order to do or not do certain acts, the seizure of any property justified by the circumstances, and liability for all costs.

paragraphs.summary: The court states it can start contempt proceedings against Olumide with severe penalties for breaching the vexatious litigant order.

propositions.text: Given the importance of vexatious litigant orders and the flagrant breach, the Court is certain it can start contempt proceedings against Ade Olumide now.
propositions.quote: this Court is certain that it can now start contempt proceedings against Ade Olumide.

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes it can now start contempt proceedings against Olumide due to the flagrant breach of the vexatious litigant order.

propositions.text: Contempt proceedings can be started but it is a discretionary call whether they should be started.
propositions.quote: just because contempt proceedings can be started does not mean that they should be started. It is a discretionary call.

paragraphs.summary: The court states contempt proceedings can be started but it is a discretionary call whether they should be started.

propositions.text: The Court examined decisions across Canada involving Ade Olumide and contempt provisions similar to ours.
propositions.quote: this Court has examined all of the decisions in various jurisdictions across Canada in which orders have been made against Ade Olumide, including all the jurisdictions in which he has been declared a vexatious litigant.

propositions.text: Ade Olumide was told about possible contempt proceedings but not about serious consequences in detail.
propositions.quote: while Ade Olumide has been told about the possibility of contempt proceedings, he has never been told in detail about the serious consequences that can follow from them.

paragraphs.summary: The court examined decisions involving Ade Olumide and found he was told about contempt proceedings but not serious consequences in detail.

propositions.text: This case is a close call but a clear and strong warning about serious consequences is appropriate here.
propositions.quote: This case is a close call. But on this one occasion, delivery of a clear and strong warning outlining the serious consequences is appropriate.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds this case a close call but a clear strong warning about serious consequences is appropriate.

propositions.text: Ade Olumide is warned that recurrence of similar conduct will lead to contempt proceedings.
propositions.quote: Ade Olumide is warned that he is playing with fire: evidence of a recurrence of the conduct here or conduct similar to it in breach of any of this Court’s orders will be met with proceedings for contempt.

propositions.text: Jennifer Virgo is warned that complicity with Ade Olumide in breaching court orders may lead to contempt proceedings against her.
propositions.quote: Jennifer Virgo is warned that if evidence arises suggesting complicity with Ade Olumide in a breach of an order of the Court, she may have contempt proceedings brought against her.

propositions.text: If found guilty of contempt, severe consequences including imprisonment and fines may apply.
propositions.quote: If those proceedings result in a guilty verdict, the potential severe consequences discussed above will all be in play.

paragraphs.summary: The court warns Ade Olumide and Jennifer Virgo about contempt proceedings and severe consequences if found guilty.

propositions.text: The Court chose to write widely accessible reasons rather than a less-accessible speaking order and questions why.
propositions.quote: In this case, the Court has chosen to write widely accessible reasons in this matter rather than issuing a less-accessible speaking order. Why?

paragraphs.summary: The court notes it chose to write widely accessible reasons rather than a less-accessible speaking order and asks why.

propositions.text: The Court wants judges and judicial officers to know Ade Olumide and Jennifer Virgo have been strongly warned to comply with court orders.
propositions.quote: The Court wants the judges and Prothonotaries in the Federal Courts system and judges and judicial officers in other jurisdictions’ courts to know that Ade Olumide and Jennifer Virgo have been given a strong warning to comply with court orders, particularly vexatious litigant orders.

propositions.text: Any doubt about the ease and consequences of contempt proceedings against Ade Olumide and Jennifer Virgo is now eliminated.
propositions.quote: all doubt has now been eliminated: Ade Olumide and Jennifer Virgo now know about the ease with which, in circumstances like these, contempt proceedings can be started and the serious consequences that can follow.

propositions.text: Ade Olumide and Jennifer Virgo now know imprisonment and substantial fines are real possibilities for contempt.
propositions.quote: In particular, they now know that a long period of imprisonment and a substantial fine are a real possibility.

propositions.text: Ignoring this warning in future may lead to dangerous proceedings for Ade Olumide and Jennifer Virgo.
propositions.quote: If, in the future, here or elsewhere, Ade Olumide, Jennifer Virgo or both ignore the warning given in these reasons, they may well find themselves enmeshed in proceedings fraught with danger.

paragraphs.summary: The court wants judges to know Ade Olumide and Jennifer Virgo have been strongly warned about contempt consequences and risks of ignoring the warning.

propositions.text: The respondent complained Ade Olumide was breaching the vexatious litigant order, which was appropriate.
propositions.quote: the respondent has complained that Ade Olumide was breaching the vexatious litigant order. The respondent was most appropriate in doing so.

propositions.text: The Court should have considered the respondent’s complaint and taken action sooner but does not criticize the respondent.
propositions.quote: Ideally, this Court should have considered the respondent’s complaint and taken action sooner. This being said, and I mean no criticism by this, right after receiving the notice of appeal the respondent could have forced the Court to deal with the breach

propositions.text: The respondent could have asked the Court to grant relief under Rule 74 or plenary power immediately after notice of appeal.
propositions.quote: the respondent could have asked the Court to grant relief under Rule 74 or its plenary power.

paragraphs.summary: The respondent complained Ade Olumide breached the vexatious litigant order; the court finds the complaint appropriate and notes the respondent could have sought relief sooner.

propositions.text: Multiple means exist to summarily terminate illegitimate or doomed proceedings in this Court, including Rule 74 and plenary power.
propositions.quote: Multiple means exist by which this Court can summarily terminate illegitimate proceedings or proceedings doomed to fail and many of these means can be pursued immediately after proceedings are started in this Court

propositions.text: References to cases illustrating the Court’s power to quash proceedings and plenary jurisdiction.
propositions.quote: see Fabrikant No. 1, above at para. 3 and Fabrikant v. Canada, 2018 FCA 224 at para. 26 (Fabrikant No. 2); for the general power to quash, see Canada (National Revenue) v. J.P. Morgan Asset Management (Canada) Inc., 2013 FCA 250, [2014] 2 F.C.R. 557, Lee v. Canada (Correctional Service), 2017 FCA 228 and Forner v. Professional Institute of the Public Service of Canada, 2016 FCA 35.

propositions.text: A search for cases where the Court exercised plenary jurisdiction will yield many useful cases.
propositions.quote: A search for cases where this Court has invoked and exercised its plenary jurisdiction will yield many more useful cases.

paragraphs.summary: The court states multiple means exist to summarily terminate illegitimate proceedings, citing cases illustrating plenary power and quashing authority.

propositions.text: Early quashing of illegitimate or hopeless proceedings frees resources for better use.
propositions.quote: The early quashing of messy, time-consuming, illegitimate or hopeless proceedings—particularly those that spawn multiple motions—can free up resources better spent elsewhere.

propositions.text: The Court recently emphasized the resource issue and proactive litigation management to root out unmeritorious cases early.
propositions.quote: Our Court has recently underscored this point (at para. 25 of Fabrikant No. 2): Most certainly there is a resource issue, even at the best of times: Olumide at paras. 17-21.

propositions.text: The Court faces a resource issue with a full docket and complex cases competing for space.
propositions.quote: The legal complement of the Court has fallen behind Canada’s population growth. Sprawling, multifarious cases with complexity as great as this Court has ever seen now vie for space in an already full, difficult docket.

propositions.text: The Court adopts proactive litigation management guided by principles to root out unmeritorious cases early and simplify others.
propositions.quote: We have tried to cope by adopting a proactive approach to litigation management guided by two principles: unnecessary and unmeritorious cases should be rooted out and quashed as early as possible—or, even better, prevented in the first place—and other cases should be simplified to the extent they can.

propositions.text: Despite efforts, resource issues remain pressing and impair timely justice.
propositions.quote: Despite this, the resource issue remains pressing, impairing litigants’ access to timely justice.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds early quashing of illegitimate cases frees resources; despite proactive management, resource issues impair timely justice.

propositions.text: Given available tools and Supreme Court encouragement, the court is baffled why illegitimate proceedings persist.
propositions.quote: Given all of the available tools and given the Supreme Court’s strong encouragement to courts and parties to develop and use tools to address this problem (see Hryniak v. Mauldin, 2014 SCC 9, [2014] 1 S.C.R. 87), I am baffled why so many messy, time-consuming, illegitimate and hopeless proceedings are allowed to fester in our court system.

paragraphs.summary: The court is baffled why illegitimate proceedings persist despite available tools and Supreme Court encouragement to address them.

propositions.text: The appeal and filing of notice of appeal are contrary to the vexatious litigant order.
propositions.quote: this appeal, and in particular the filing of the notice of appeal, are contrary to the vexatious litigant order.

propositions.text: Under Rule 74 and plenary power, the notice of appeal is ordered removed and the file closed.
propositions.quote: Therefore, under Rule 74 and this Court’s plenary power, I would order that the notice of appeal be removed from the file and the file closed.

propositions.text: The respondent does not seek global costs of the appeal.
propositions.quote: The respondent does not seek its global costs of the appeal.

paragraphs.summary: The court orders removal of the notice of appeal and file closure under Rule 74 and plenary power; respondent does not seek global costs.

propositions.text: The respondent requests an order prohibiting Ade Olumide from representing or conducting litigation for others.
propositions.quote: The respondent also requests an order that Ade Olumide be prohibited from representing or otherwise conducting litigation on behalf of his spouse or any other individual.

propositions.text: This request goes beyond the vexatious litigant order's prohibition on starting new proceedings without leave.
propositions.quote: This goes a little beyond the prohibition contained in the vexatious litigant order against Ade Olumide against starting new proceedings without leave, whether acting for himself or through others

propositions.text: The requested order would prevent Ade Olumide from conducting litigation for others regardless of his interest.
propositions.quote: the requested order would prevent Ade Olumide from conducting litigation for another party in any circumstance regardless of whether he has an interest in the litigation.

paragraphs.summary: The respondent requests an order prohibiting Ade Olumide from representing others, which goes beyond the vexatious litigant order's scope.

propositions.text: Under plenary power and Rule 55, the court would make the requested order prohibiting Ade Olumide from conducting litigation for others without leave.
propositions.quote: Under the Court’s plenary power to prevent abuses and Rule 55, I would make the requested order.

propositions.text: Rule 119 prohibits Ade Olumide from representing others without leave of the Court.
propositions.quote: Rule 119 already prohibits Ade Olumide from representing others unless he gets leave of the Court.

propositions.text: The requested order is broader than Rule 119 but justified given Ade Olumide's breaches and vexatious litigant status.
propositions.quote: The requested order is somewhat broader than that envisaged by Rule 119 but is justified in these special circumstances: absent leave, a vexatious litigant of this sort, especially one who has breached a vexatious litigant order, should not be participating in litigation in any way whatsoever, absent leave of this Court.

paragraphs.summary: The court would order Ade Olumide prohibited from conducting litigation for others without leave, broader than Rule 119 but justified here.

propositions.text: A motion within this appeal led to submissions under Rule 74 but the Court has not decided the motion.
propositions.quote: It will be recalled that the bringing of a motion within this appeal led this Court to call for submissions under Rule 74. The Court has not decided this motion.

propositions.text: Since the appeal no longer exists, the motion must be dismissed.
propositions.quote: Since the appeal before this Court will no longer exist, the motion must necessarily be dismissed.

propositions.text: The respondent seeks costs on the motion, which is appropriate.
propositions.quote: On the motion, the respondent seeks his costs. That is appropriate.

propositions.text: The court would dismiss the motion with costs.
propositions.quote: Therefore, I would dismiss the motion with costs.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes a motion under Rule 74 is undecided but must be dismissed as the appeal ends; respondent seeks and is awarded costs.
